beats.narration: Investor day went well. Very well. Sprout Labs now has money, a manufacturing partner, and a promise to ship five thousand connected Sprouts by autumn.
Connected! Owners will see their plant's moisture on their phones. They will get alerts. We will push new features while they sleep!
Every one of those sentences makes me nervous.
Connecting a device changes everything. It can now be reached by its owner, by its makers, and by anyone else on the internet who is curious, bored, or malicious.
Today: building a connected device that stays robust and safe.
Each wireless option trades range, power, cost, and convenience. Wi-Fi is everywhere in homes, but power hungry. Bluetooth Low Energy sips power, but needs a phone nearby.
Cellular works anywhere, at a monthly cost.
We pick Wi-Fi for the data, and Bluetooth for setup. The phone app connects over Bluetooth, hands Sprout the Wi-Fi password, and gets out of the way.
A connected device usually talks to a cloud server, not directly to the phone. The server stores history, sends alerts, and relays commands.
That makes the server part of the product, and its failures become the device's failures.
What happens when the internet goes down?
Sprout must keep watering. Offline is normal, not an emergency. The connected features are a bonus layered on top of a device that works on its own.
Offline-first has practical consequences. Sprout stores its readings locally while disconnected and uploads them later, in order, when the connection returns.
Its clock must keep reasonable time without the network, and it must never wait on the server before making a watering decision.
Wi-Fi also costs power. Connecting to a router can take a few seconds at full current. So Sprout does not stay connected.
It wakes, connects, sends a batch of readings, checks for messages, and disconnects.
Batching is the key idea. One connection every hour, carrying sixty readings, costs far less energy than sixty connections carrying one reading each.
We will dig into the power math in a later episode.
Networks lose messages, duplicate them, deliver them late, and occasionally corrupt them. Robust communication plans for all of it.
Version numbers matter more than people expect. Next year, the message format will change. Old Sprouts and new servers must still understand each other.

visual.title: Rules for robust messages

Every message has a sequence number
Important messages need acknowledgement
Retry with increasing delays
Handle duplicates gracefully
Check integrity with a CRC

beats.narration: A version field in every message lets each side know what it is reading.

beats.narration: Sequence numbers detect lost and duplicated messages. If the server receives report forty-one twice, it ignores the second. If it never receives forty-two, it can ask for it.

visual.title: A message header
lines: uint8_t  version;     // format version, starts at 1
uint16_t length;      // bytes of payload that follow
uint32_t sequence;    // detects loss and duplicates
>  uint32_t crc;         // integrity check over all of it

beats.narration: And retries should back off. If a thousand Sprouts lose the server at once and all retry every second, they knock it over again the moment it comes back.

uint16_t length;      // bytes of payload that follow
uint32_t sequence;    // detects loss and duplicates
>  uint32_t crc;         // integrity check over all of it

beats.narration: A CRC, or cyclic redundancy check, is a short number computed from a block of data. The sender computes it and attaches it. The receiver computes it again.
If they differ, the data changed in transit.
A CRC is excellent at catching accidental errors, like flipped bits from noise. A thirty-two bit CRC catches all short bursts of errors and almost all random ones.
But a CRC is not a security measure. Anyone who changes the data on purpose can just compute a new CRC. Detecting tampering requires cryptography.
So the CRC is like a seal on a jar. It shows if the jar was dropped, not if someone carefully resealed it.
That is surprisingly accurate, Cy.
Connected devices need two security properties above all. Confidentiality: nobody else can read the messages. And authenticity: messages really come from who they claim, unchanged.
For network traffic, we use a standard secure protocol, the same family your web browser uses. We do not invent our own cryptography. Ever.
Why not? I bet I could make a clever cipher.
Because the hard part of cryptography is not scrambling data. It is all the small mistakes around it: reused nonces, weak random numbers, timing leaks, broken key handling.
Random numbers deserve a special mention. Keys and nonces must be unpredictable.
A microcontroller that seeds its random generator from the same value at every boot produces the same keys on every unit.
Use a hardware random number generator if the chip has one.
Everyone thinks that, and almost everyone is wrong. Standard algorithms have survived decades of attacks by experts. Homemade ones usually survive until the first curious teenager.
Keys matter as much as algorithms. If every Sprout shares one secret key, extracting it from one unit compromises all five thousand.
Each device should have its own identity, created during manufacturing and stored where it is hard to read out.
Before adding security features at random, the team does a risk analysis: what are we protecting, from whom, and what happens if we fail?
For each threat, we estimate how bad it would be and how likely. Then we spend effort where the product of the two is largest.
The scary one is not someone overwatering a fern. It is someone using five thousand Sprouts as a botnet, or stealing the Wi-Fi passwords of five thousand homes.
Notice the device holds the owner's Wi-Fi password. That makes Sprout a guest in someone's home network, with all the responsibility of a guest.
Treat that data like it matters, because it does.
Can we skip the security stuff for version one and add it later?
Security added later is usually security never added. And some of it, like unique keys, can only be done at the factory. We do it now.
The most powerful feature of a connected device is the ability to update its firmware remotely. It is also the most dangerous.
A bad update can turn five thousand working devices into five thousand plant-shaped bricks.
The safe design uses a small bootloader that never changes, and two slots for firmware. The device runs from slot A while it downloads the new version into slot B.
If power fails during download, nothing is lost: the old firmware is untouched.

visual.title: A safe update
items: Download the new image to the spare slot
Verify its size, CRC, and signature
Mark it as try once
Reboot into the new image
New image runs its self test
If healthy, mark it confirmed
If not, bootloader falls back to the old slot

beats.narration: If the new firmware crashes on boot, the bootloader notices it was never confirmed, and goes back to the old slot.

beats.narration: That old slot is the lifeboat. As long as it is there and intact, no update can sink the ship.

beats.narration: How does Sprout know an update really came from Sprout Labs? Not from an attacker who got onto the network? Digital signatures.
Sprout Labs signs each image with a private key that never leaves a locked-down server. Every device holds the matching public key, which can check signatures but cannot make them.
The bootloader verifies the signature before running anything. Firmware without a valid signature is rejected, no matter how it arrived.
Guard that private key with your life. If it leaks, attackers can sign anything. And plan how you would replace it, before you ever need to.
Also, block downgrades. Otherwise an attacker could install an old, genuine, signed firmware that has a known security hole.
Right. Each image carries a version number inside the signed part, and the bootloader refuses anything older than what is installed.
A small counter in protected memory remembers the minimum allowed version.
Secure boot ties it together. From the first instruction after reset, each stage verifies the next before running it: the bootloader verifies the application, and nothing unverified ever executes.
Even a verified, signed, well-tested update can have a bug that only appears in real homes. So you never update everyone at once.
Start with one percent of devices, ideally including your own. Watch crash reports, connection rates, and battery drain. If all is well, expand to five, then twenty-five, then everyone.
Each stage is a checkpoint. A bad update that reaches one percent of devices is an embarrassing week. One that reaches everyone at once can end a company.
One percent? But the new feature is ready now!
And it will still be ready in a week, Cy. With five thousand happy customers instead of five thousand angry ones.
With thousands of devices, new problems appear. The fleet needs monitoring: which versions are running where, which units crash, which ones went quiet.
Spread out the check-ins. If every Sprout reports at exactly midnight, the server gets five thousand visitors in one second and falls over.

visual.title: Fleet basics
items: Report firmware version on connect
Upload crash records
Track battery and signal health
Spread out check-in times
Have a plan to retire devices

beats.narration: And it all starts at the factory. Each unit must be programmed, tested, given its unique identity and keys, and recorded, all in a few minutes on a production line.

beats.narration: The factory test uses the command line we built in episode three. The same commands, run automatically by a test station.
If any step fails, that unit goes to a repair bin, not into a box.
Factories have their own constraints. Every second on the line costs money, so programming and testing must be fast.
Test fixtures with spring pins press against test pads on the board, so no one has to plug in cables by hand.
And the factory must be able to tell us which unit failed which test, months later, by serial number.
When a batch of field returns appears, those records tell you whether it was a bad batch of parts or a design problem.
Can we just skip the test for the cheap units?
Every unit is the cheap unit, Cy. That is the point of manufacturing.
To recap. Choose a connection that fits your device's range and power budget, and make sure it works offline.
